intro: Cassano d'Adda is a town on the river Adda east of Milan. In its quarter of Taranta, in front of a row of houses, grows an old pollarded mulberry whose thick grey arms rise from a gnarled trunk like the fingers of an open hand. A reader photographed it, sent it to us and puts it at 400 years old.

question_answer: The Old Mulberry of Taranta stands in front of houses in the Taranta quarter of Cassano d'Adda. It can be seen from the street; the ground around it is not open to visitors.
question_context: A reader sent us this mulberry from Taranta, a quarter of Cassano d'Adda on the Adda east of Milan, and puts it at about 400 years old. That figure is theirs; we have not found a record of the tree. The photograph shows a tree shaped by centuries of cutting. A short, dark, gnarled trunk, split and swollen low down, carries a ring of thick grey arms that rise like the fingers of an open hand, each ending in a tuft of fresh leaves where it was pruned back. That is pollarding, the old way of cropping a mulberry for its leaves, and across Lombardy mulberries were once kept like this in great numbers to feed silkworms. Metal props help hold the arms, a small sign stands in front of the trunk and a clipped hedge surrounds it. The reader calls it a black mulberry; the leaves could be black or white mulberry, and we ask readers to tell us which. It stands in front of private houses, so the way to see it is from the street.

trees.story:
A reader sent us this mulberry from Taranta, a quarter of Cassano d'Adda on the river Adda east of Milan, and puts it at 400 years old. That is their figure; we have not found a record of the tree yet.

What the photograph shows is a tree that has been worked for a very long time. Its trunk is short, dark and gnarled, swollen and split low down, and from its top a ring of thick grey arms rises like the fingers of an open hand, each ending in a fresh green tuft where it has been cut back. That is pollarding, the old way of cropping a mulberry for its leaves, and across Lombardy mulberries were once kept like this by the thousand to feed silkworms. Metal props now help hold up the arms, a small sign stands in front of the trunk, and a clipped hedge rings it on a corner between the houses.

The reader calls it a black mulberry. The leaves in the picture could belong to the black or to the white, the silk farmers' tree; if you know which it is, tell us here.

It stands in front of private houses, so take it in from the street.
